content: DOCK8, also known as Dedicator of Cytokinesis 8 or Zir3, is a large protein with a molecular weight of approximately 190 kDa. It plays a critical role in intracellular signaling pathways. DOCK8 belongs to the DOCK-C subfamily of the DOCK family of guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs), which are responsible for activating small G proteins. DOCK8 was initially discovered through a yeast two-hybrid (YTH) screening process aimed at identifying proteins that interact with the Rho family small G protein, Cdc42. Subsequent northern blot analyses demonstrated that DOCK8 is highly expressed in tissues such as the placenta, lung, kidney, and pancreas, with lower expression levels observed in the heart, brain, and skeletal muscle. Structurally, DOCK8 shares the same core domain organization as other members of the DOCK protein family. It contains a DHR2 domain, which in other proteins is known to mediate guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) activity, and a DHR1 domain, which interacts with phospholipids in other proteins. In the YTH system, DOCK8 was shown to interact with the small G proteins Rac1 and Cdc42. However, stable interactions between DOCK8 and these G proteins were not observed in GST-pulldown assays. This lack of stable interaction may be due to the requirement for adaptor proteins to stabilize the complex and facilitate nucleotide exchange, a characteristic of many DOCK-G protein interactions. Mutations in the DOCK8 gene are associated with the autosomal recessive form of Job's syndrome, also known as hyper-IgE syndrome (HIES). This condition typically manifests in infancy, with affected individuals surviving into late childhood or adolescence. Clinical features of this syndrome include eczema, recurrent cold staphylococcal abscesses, recurrent lung infections, coarse facial features (thickened skin), retention of primary teeth (resulting in two rows of teeth), elevated IgE levels, and eosinophilia. Although the precise cellular role of DOCK8 remains incompletely understood, its significance has been highlighted in various studies. Disruptions in the DOCK8 gene have been implicated in several diseases. For example, deletion or reduced expression of DOCK8 has been reported in a human lung cancer cell line. Additionally, DOCK8 has been identified as a potential candidate gene associated with the progression of gliomas. Autosomal recessive DOCK8 deficiency is a specific variant of combined immunodeficiency and a distinct form of hyper-IgE syndrome. This condition, first described in 2004, is caused by biallelic germline mutations in the DOCK8 gene. The clinical presentation of DOCK8 deficiency differs from other forms of HIES and is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Patients with DOCK8 deficiency experience recurrent infections, allergies, and malignancies. Nearly all affected individuals suffer from recurrent or chronic infections of the upper and lower respiratory tracts, often necessitating sinus surgery or the placement of myringotomy tubes. Recurrent lung infections can lead to bronchiectasis, a condition characterized by widened and scarred airways. Cutaneous infections in DOCK8 deficiency are particularly severe and challenging to treat. These include viral infections such as herpes simplex virus, human papillomavirus, and molluscum contagiosum; bacterial infections, particularly with Staphylococcus aureus; and fungal infections of the skin or oral mucosa caused by Candida species. Eczema is a common feature and can be severe, often complicated by secondary bacterial infections. These skin infections can become disfiguring over time. Patients with DOCK8 deficiency frequently exhibit allergies to various foods and environmental allergens, as well as asthma. Autoimmune manifestations, such as autoimmune hemolytic anemia, vasculitis, and vasculopathy, have also been observed. Additionally, individuals with this condition are at an increased risk of developing malignancies, including squamous cell carcinomas and lymphoid cancers. Some lymphomas in these patients are associated with poor control of the Epstein–Barr virus, a known oncogenic virus. Given the significant cancer risks, close monitoring for signs of malignancy is essential. DOCK8 deficiency is classified as a combined immunodeficiency because it involves both reduced lymphocyte numbers and impaired lymphocyte function. It is also considered a type of autosomal recessive hyper-IgE syndrome. Laboratory findings in affected individuals include progressive lymphopenia, primarily affecting CD4 and CD8 T cell subsets, as well as reduced B cell and/or natural killer (NK) cell counts in some cases. Eosinophilia and abnormalities in immunoglobulin levels are also common. Antibody responses to vaccines are often poor. Loss of DOCK8 protein expression can be confirmed through diagnostic intracellular flow cytometry testing. Treatment for DOCK8 deficiency is tailored to the individual’s clinical condition and typically involves managing infections, allergies, and asthma. Interferon-alpha has been used to control severe viral infections, such as widespread warts or herpes simplex virus. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is a curative option for many primary immunodeficiencies and has been successfully employed in patients with DOCK8 deficiency.
